mcqs.question: What does the driver/navigator model in a pairing interview typically involve?
options: One person types and narrates while the other reads, questions, and suggests direction, usually inside an existing repo
Both candidates write separate solutions independently and compare at the end
The interviewer types while the candidate only watches and answers questions
The candidate works entirely alone with the interviewer observing silently
mcqs.explanation: Driver/navigator splits typing from directing, with roles usually swapping partway through inside a codebase the interviewer already knows. The other options describe formats that aren't genuine pairing at all — independent work, interviewer-as-driver, or silent solo observation.

mcqs.question: In a pairing round, which is more likely to score higher: a fast, technically correct solution built while ignoring the interviewer's input, or a slightly slower solution built collaboratively?
options: The fast solo-style solution, since correctness is the only thing that matters
Neither — speed and collaboration are weighted equally regardless of context
It depends entirely on which one finishes the stated task first
The slower, collaborative solution, since collaboration and adaptability are core parts of the signal
mcqs.explanation: Pairing rounds explicitly evaluate collaboration and adaptability alongside correctness — a correct answer built while tuning out the partner misses most of what the format tests. Finishing first isn't the deciding factor when collaboration is a primary signal.

mcqs.question: You notice a function in the existing codebase does two unrelated things and would benefit from a refactor, but it's outside the scope of your assigned task. What's the best move?
options: Silently refactor it as part of your change since you already noticed the problem
Ignore it completely and never mention it
Name it out loud and ask whether to include it in scope or just note it
Refuse to touch any code near it until it's refactored first
mcqs.explanation: Naming the observation and checking scope respects the time budget and mirrors real teamwork — silently refactoring eats limited time on an unstated goal, ignoring it wastes a genuine observation, and refusing to proceed is an overreaction to a minor issue.

mcqs.question: You're 20 minutes into a 45-minute pairing round and still reading through the codebase without having written code. What's the strongest response?
options: Say nothing and keep reading until you feel fully confident in the codebase
Say out loud that you're behind schedule and propose starting implementation now
Silently switch to a completely different, simpler task
Ask the interviewer to extend the round to make up the lost time
mcqs.explanation: Naming the time pressure and proposing to move forward demonstrates exactly the time-awareness pairing rounds reward. Continuing to read silently burns more time, switching tasks unilaterally sidesteps the interviewer, and assuming an extension isn't a reliable option.

mcqs.question: The interviewer suggests a different approach than the one you've already started. What response best fits what a pairing round is testing?
options: Continue with your original plan without acknowledging the suggestion
Immediately abandon your approach and adopt theirs without discussion
Genuinely consider it out loud, then explain your reasoning whichever way you go
Politely note it but privately keep implementing your own plan unchanged
mcqs.explanation: Engaging with the suggestion — even if you end up keeping your original approach — is what the round evaluates; the reasoning process matters more than which approach wins. Ignoring it, blindly switching, or silently disregarding it after a polite nod all skip the genuine collaboration being tested.
